title: hdtp-identity: the library boundary
description: Every function a port of hdtp-identity presents, as `call(name, args) -> answer`: what it takes, what it answers, and which error codes it can fail with. This file is the source; CONTRACT.md is rendered from it and js/parity.mjs holds both ports to it.

why.description: One line, in this library's own words — never another library's error text, which a second port could not reproduce.

ErrorCode.description: Why a call failed. `bad_request`: an argument is missing or unusable as asked. `parse`: bytes that are there and will not read. `unsupported`: an algorithm or a function this library does not have. `envelope_invalid`: SPEC §12's code, for an envelope that does not open or prove itself. `vault`: the vault refused. `root_expired`: a wallet asked to sign under a root past its `notAfter` (SPEC §2.2) — the library's refusal, never a code on the wire; a verifier meeting such a root in a chain refuses it by rule 4 of `validate_chain`. `key` and `internal` are declared so a caller's switch has a name for them; no input known reaches either.

B64url.description: Bytes, as base64url without padding, in exactly this alphabet. Every answer spells them this way, and every wire object of the specification is read this strictly: an envelope's members, an export's certificates, a signing request. A library argument outside those objects is also read with padding or the standard alphabet, and never with whitespace (CONTRACT §0); a card's certificate loses its spaces, tabs, CRs and LFs before it is read (`card_decode`).

Alg.description: A key algorithm. A key of any other is refused where it is read (CONTRACT §0).

Fingerprint.description: `"sha256:" + b64url(SHA-256(SPKI))`, in its one spelling: the last character's two spare bits are zero (RFC 4648 §3.5).

Instant.description: An RFC 3339 UTC instant with second precision, as every answer writes one.

InstantIn.description: An RFC 3339 UTC instant as an argument, in the one grammar every port reads: upper-case T and Z, no offset, `.` alone before a fraction of a second, which is allowed and DROPPED, because the boundary is whole seconds.

Tbs.description: A TBSCertificate, DER: the bytes an external signer signs.

SigAlg.description: An AlgorithmIdentifier, DER — the TBS's own third field.

Serial.description: A certificate serial number, 8 to 20 bytes. Absent, the core draws 8 random bytes.

Form.description: How the sender proves itself inside the plaintext: its whole chain, or the fingerprint of a leaf the recipient already holds.

Envelope.description: A sealed envelope: its four members (SPEC §13.1).

ArrivedEnvelope.description: An envelope as it ARRIVED: four strings, which may be anything. Judging their spelling is the function's work, not the caller's.

key_usage.description: The bit positions that are set.

extensions.description: Every extension in the order the certificate carries them.

Certificate.description: A certificate read back. `profile_error` judges it as a root when it is self-issued and a CA, otherwise as a leaf.

leaf_fingerprint.description: Which leaf this pin holds (§5). Optional: with it, only the pin that matched is parsed.

Pin.description: A contact as the host holds it. `state` absent is `active`; any other value but the three is refused, as is a `leaf_fingerprint` that is not a fingerprint (NodeState).

Windows.description: The protocol's windows, in seconds unless named otherwise, as both ports hold them (a test in each holds its constants to these, and a host that needs one reads it here): `skew_s`, how far a received envelope's `ts` may be from now, and `max_lifetime_s`, the most `exp − ts` may be (SPEC §13.3); `tombstone_s`, how long a removal tombstone holds a returning root at `ask` (§5.3), and `claim_window_s`, how long an endpoint stays claimed by the root that was pinned at it (§5.2) — each an age strictly under the window; `max_leaf_days`, the longest leaf a verifier accepts (§14.2); `signing_max_ahead_s`, the furthest ahead a signing request may expire (§9.1).

CanonicalNumbers.description: How the canonical JSON of an envelope header and a vault's authenticated data writes a number (RFC 8785 §3.2.2.3: as ECMAScript's Number prints it). Each row is a JSON number as a caller may write it and the text both ports canonicalise it to; a test in each port runs every row.

NodeState.description: What the host knows, handed to `decide` whole. Every list absent is empty; `accept_new_hosts` absent is `auto`, and anything but `auto` or `ask` is refused (`node.accept_new_hosts is auto or ask`). Read member by member in this order, a held key as `kid`, `leaf`, `pkcs8`, `current`, a pin as `root`, `endpoint`, `leaf`, `state`, `leaf_fingerprint`, a tombstone as `root`, `leaf`, `at`, a former endpoint as `root`, `endpoint`, `at`: a member absent, null or of the wrong type where one is required is `bad_request` naming it by its path (`node.endpoint is required`, `node.keys[0].kid is required`, `node.seen[1] is required`), and a pin's, a tombstone's or a former endpoint's `root` that is not a fingerprint is `bad_request` `<path>.root is not a fingerprint` (`node.pins[0].root is not a fingerprint`), read where the root is: the host's damaged state, which read as a root nothing matched came back as an `address_claim` that was not a fingerprint. So, each where it is read, is a held key's `kid` that is not a fingerprint (`<path>.kid is not a fingerprint`), a pin's `state` other than `active`, `pending_out` or `blocked` (`<path>.state is active, pending_out or blocked`; one was read as `active`, so a blocked contact whose host wrote `Blocked` was a full contact), and a pin's `leaf_fingerprint` that is not a fingerprint (`<path>.leaf_fingerprint is not a fingerprint`; `""` was a claim matching no leaf in one port and no claim in the other). The typed `decide` and `decide_chain` ask the same of a typed caller's state first, in the reader's order, where a Go caller's zero values, a `state` or a `leaf_fingerprint` of `""`, are `active` and none.

GuestWhy.description: Why a caller proven by a chain is a guest: its root is not pinned (`unknown root`), its pin is blocked (`blocked`), or the leaf it signed with is older than the pinned one (`superseded leaf`, §14.3). The words are the seed's `receive()`'s.

Decision.description: What `decide` decided. `code` says which shape this is, and for `ok`, `tier`: a guest is answered with the reason it is one and whether a pin stands behind it.

demote.description: True exactly when a pin for `root` stands in the node state and the caller is served as a guest anyway (`why` `blocked` or `superseded leaf`): nothing the call does is the contact's, and a host resolves the caller to no contact row. A host reads this member, never the words of `why`.

oneOf.description: A `pending_out` pin calling anything but the pending tier's tools: the call waits for the owner's approval. It names what the signature proved — `root`, `endpoint`, the `leaf` it verified under and the `form` — and the request's `msg_id`, which no `seen` effect carries here, so a host can seal the refusal back to the caller (§13.2) without opening the envelope again. The pin's own moves are effects; `seen` is not one, since the call was not taken.

Effect.description: Something the host must apply. `decide` changes nothing itself. `seen` is the envelope's; the rest are the pins' (`PinEffect`).

PinEffect.description: What the pins decided a host must apply — the moves of a pin, a former endpoint, an event, a new address waiting for the owner: what `decide` and `decide_chain` both answer. `decide` changes nothing itself, and neither does `decide_chain`.

ChainDecision.description: What `decide_chain` decided about a chain proven outside an envelope: `decide`'s answer to the same chain and node, less what is the call's (`method`, `tool`, `params`, `form`) and less the envelope's own refusals. A guest carries its reason, `demote` and the address claim; a chain that fails a rule, or a leaf of the pinned one's notBefore that is not it, is `envelope_invalid` in `decide`'s words.

Kdf.description: The key derivation, as a vault DOCUMENT carries it: all four members, each inside its range. The ranges are checked at both ends on both paths, by one parser — an unbounded reader hands an attacker's file a 256 GiB allocation, and an unbounded writer seals a person's root behind a KDF a laptop brute-forces. A value that does not fit in 32 bits is out of range, never truncated.

KdfArgs.description: The same, as an ARGUMENT to `vault_seal`: every member may be left out and takes `KdfDefault`'s, and what is given is held to the same range as a document's.

KdfDefault.description: The key derivation `vault_seal` uses for a member its caller leaves out: 64 MiB, three passes, one lane. A test in each port holds its default to this, and its bounds to `Kdf`'s and `KdfArgs`'s.

VaultSaltMin.description: The shortest salt, in bytes, that a vault document or `vault_seal`'s `salt` may carry: Argon2id's own floor, named by both ports before Argon2id is asked for anything (`vault`, `salt is at least 8 bytes`), at both ends. A test in each port holds its constant to this.

SigningRequest.description: A host's signing request (SPEC §9.1), the members of its form as the form carries them: every one a string. Bounds are bytes, and characters (Unicode scalar values) for `recipient`; the whole body is bounded by the wallet's host.

csr.description: base64url PKCS #10: the recipient's key and the endpoint.

root_cert.description: base64url DER of the root, if the host holds it.

redirect.description: Where the answer goes: https, or http to a loopback host; no userinfo, no fragment.

recipient.description: What the host calls itself: shown as its claim, never trusted.

valid_days.description: The validity the host asks for, 1 to 398, as the form's text: a suggestion; the person chooses.

expires.description: RFC 3339 UTC, after now and at most ten minutes ahead.

ExportLimits.description: The bounds of SPEC §9.2, in bytes unless named otherwise. A host counts the bytes it actually decompresses against them; the core holds the directory's sizes and the text it is handed to them. A host also sets a whole-file ceiling of its own, and names it when it refuses.

files.description: The text members to the sha256 of their bytes. Never a media member: each is bound by its name, the sha256 of its bytes, and counted by counts.media.

ContactRow.description: One row of contacts.csv (SPEC §9.2), as JSON: the permissions as lists, was_active a boolean, an empty leaf or root_cert null.

ThreadRow.description: One row of threads.csv (SPEC §9.2). A removed thread is one whose contact is no root of contacts.csv: a former contact's conversation, which carries the names the contact is known by; on any other thread the two names are empty, and export_read does not answer them.

contact_name.description: On a removed thread, the name the owner last gave the contact, at most 200 characters.

contact_display_name.description: On a removed thread, the name the contact last gave themselves, at most 200 characters.

MessageRow.description: One line of messages.jsonl (SPEC §9.2): at most one attachment, and a message with one has an empty body.

DirectoryEntry.description: One entry of the zip's central directory, as the host read it: the name as stored, the uncompressed size the header states, whether the entry is encrypted (general-purpose flag bit 0), and its Unix mode (the external attributes' high 16 bits; 0 when there is none).

LedgerEntry.description: One leaf the wallet issued: the endpoint and the dates, which is what every rule reads. Never the leaf itself, which is the host's to serve and grants nothing (SPEC §9).

VaultRoot.description: One identity the wallet holds. In the file it carries the root's key (`pkcs8`) or names the card that does (`holder`); in the record it carries neither, until the root is re-bound (SPEC §9): then `rebound_at` (ms) marks the entry and `pkcs8` stays with it.

VaultPasskey.description: The credential a derived root belongs to (SPEC §2.1); not secret.

VaultContact.description: The wallet's own copy of one contact (SPEC §9): pinned by root, at an endpoint, under the person's name; a leaf and the root certificate when the wallet has seen them.

VaultPlaintext.description: What the FILE seals: the root and nothing else (SPEC §9). `prf` is the §2.1 secret a derived root's record is opened with, for the wallet that has lost its credential. A `v` that is not 1 is refused at both ends and nothing converts.

RecordPlaintext.description: What the RECORD seals (SPEC §9): the ledger and the contact book, the roots without their keys — or with one, once a root has been re-bound — and what the wallet page keeps beside them. Under the store key of §2.1 for a wallet with a credential; beside the file, under the recovery key, for one without.

LimitsRules.description: The numbers of SPEC §12's call budgets, as a host keeps them in its configuration. Every member is required; the library holds no default.

contact_calls_per_second.description: One contact, inbound, and one contact, outbound: the sustained rate. Above 0.

contact_burst.description: How many calls a contact may make at once. At least 1, and at most 3600 seconds of `contact_calls_per_second`, so the bucket refills within the hour an idle row is kept.

identity_capacity_per_second.description: The most calls a second one identity takes from all its contacts together, and sends to all of them together. At least 1.

guest_calls_per_hour.description: A guest, per proven root and source (burst the same). At least 1.

guest_source_calls_per_hour.description: A source alone: a small form answered `chain_required` (burst the same). At least 1.

stranger_calls_out_per_hour.description: Calls out to anybody who is not an active contact, per identity (burst the same). At least 1.

integration_calls_per_hour.description: One integration, per contact (SPEC §5.7; burst the same). At least 1.

guest_total_calls_per_hour.description: Every guest together, per identity, charged before the envelope is opened (burst the same). At least 1.

pending_in_cap.description: The most contact requests an identity holds waiting on its owner.

LimitsCharge.description: What one call is charged to. The bucket keys are the cloud's `rate_buckets` keys.

oneOf.description: An active contact calling in: `contact:<root>`, then `identity` at `contact_cap` × `contact_calls_per_second`, at most `identity_capacity_per_second` and at least 1, with one second of that as its burst.

Anybody else calling in, by the root its envelope proved and the host's name for its source: `guest:<root>:<source>` when `addressed`, `guest:<root>` when not, `source:<source>` when no root was proven (absent, null or empty).
Every guest together, before the envelope is opened: `guest-total`.
A call out to an active contact: `out:contact:<root>`, then `out:identity`.
A call out to anybody who is not an active contact, or one that starts or answers a relationship: `out:stranger`.
A call to one integration by one contact: `integration:<integration>:<contact>`.
A contact request, while the identity holds `held` already: a count, no bucket.

LimitsRow.description: A bucket's row: the tokens left when it was last charged, and when, in milliseconds.

LimitsIdle.description: How long, in milliseconds, a bucket's row may sit untouched before it is full whatever it budgets: a host may delete a row older than this, and `limits_rules_check` refuses rules whose contact bucket takes longer to refill from empty (crates/hdtp-limits `IDLE_MS`, go/limits.go `LimitsIdleMS`; a test in each holds it to this).

version.notes: The build, not a rule: `spec` is the version of hdtp-spec's specification the port implements and is the same everywhere; the other member names the port's own release, so the answers differ and nothing compares them.

key_from_seed.notes: An Ed25519 seed is used directly; a P-256 scalar is the seed mod n, with 0 → 1 (the seed library's `keys.mjs`). Written for the vectors, and production API since SPEC §2.1: it is how a wallet turns a derived seed into its root.

prf_salt.notes: SPEC §2.1's fixed PRF input, `SHA-256("hdtp/vault/1")`, and the three `info` strings. A call rather than a constant a caller copies, so the bytes live in one place and the vectors prove them.

derive_seed.notes: `HKDF-SHA256(ikm = prf, salt = "", info, L = 32)`. **Refuses an `info` outside the three, and a `prf` that is not 32 bytes.** Both refusals are the point rather than hygiene: a mistyped domain separator would otherwise return 32 perfectly good bytes and silently derive an identity belonging to nobody, which is the one failure the derived-root design exists to prevent.

key_info.notes: `key_id` is the 32 raw bytes of the fingerprint's hash.

sign.notes: Ed25519 pure, or ECDSA P-256/SHA-256 in ASN.1 DER, **always the low-S twin** (`s ≤ n/2`, SPEC §14.1): a library returns either twin of an ECDSA signature, and a port returns one.

not_after.description: The identity's end date, which its person chose (SPEC §14.1). Absent or null, the root never expires: `99991231235959Z`. Before `not_before` is refused (`bad_request`, `not_after is before not_before`); one already past is the wallet's to refuse, since only the wallet knows the time.

build_root.notes: Members are read in their declared order: `cn`, `pkcs8`, `not_before`, `not_after`, `serial`.

not_after.description: The identity's end date, which its person chose (SPEC §14.1). Absent or null, the root never expires: `99991231235959Z`. Before `not_before` is refused (`bad_request`, `not_after is before not_before`); one already past is the wallet's to refuse, since only the wallet knows the time.

root_tbs.notes: The external-signing seam: a root in a passkey or a security key signs `tbs` in the host, and `assemble_root` builds the certificate from the signature handed back.

assemble_root.notes: `sig_alg` is read from the TBS; when one is handed back it must be equal, so the algorithm outside a certificate can never differ from the one inside. **An ECDSA `sig` is normalised to its low-S twin** before assembling: what arrives at the seam was made by a token or a KMS that has never heard of §14.1, and swapping a signature for its twin needs no key. Anything that is not an ECDSA value passes through untouched.

dns_name.description: The endpoint's host as a dNSName beside its URI. Absent or null is none; present and empty is refused (`dns_name is empty`).

build_leaf.notes: A raw profile builder, for tests and the vectors: it judges no date against a root and no root against the clock, so it builds a leaf that outlives its root or starts after it, which a verifier must refuse. A wallet issues through `issue_from_csr`, `issue_tbs_from_csr` or `wallet_issue`, which do. Refuses a validity over 398 days and an endpoint that is not an https URL in normal form.

dns_name.description: The endpoint's host as a dNSName beside its URI. Absent or null is none; present and empty is refused (`dns_name is empty`).

leaf_tbs.notes: The same seam for leaves: `build_leaf` with the root's public key in place of its private one, and as raw: for tests and the vectors, never a wallet's way to issue.

parse_certificate.notes: Parsing itself refuses, with a `parse` error, what DER has one encoding for and the certificate spells another way: the AlgorithmIdentifier inside the TBS differing from the one outside (`signature algorithm inside and outside differ`), a BOOLEAN that is not `0xFF` or is an explicit FALSE, a non-minimal INTEGER, an OBJECT IDENTIFIER with a padded subidentifier, a `keyUsage` BIT STRING whose unused bits are set or whose trailing zero bits are not removed, a validity of other than two times, an extension of other than two or three parts or whose value is not an OCTET STRING (`certificate shape`) or whose OCTET STRING holds more than one TLV, a P-256 key that is not the uncompressed point. Every one of these is a scenario in `vectors/intrude.mjs`, which the seed and both ports answer alike — the seed's strictness and the ports' are one rule, proven rather than asserted. A `keyUsage` BIT STRING with no initial octet (`03 00`; X.690 §8.6.2) is `BIT STRING not in the DER form`, and an `[3]` with nothing in it `not a v3 certificate with extensions`, in the seed and both ports. Both ports read a certificate's fields in one order, so one with two faults is named for the same one: the version, the serial, the validity's count, the outer algorithm's shape and its equality with the inner one, the key, the signature algorithm, the issuer, the subject, the two times, then the extensions, each extension's criticality before its OID. The seed's `parse` reads them in another order — the two algorithms' equality before the serial and the validity's count, and the key after the names and the two times — so there a certificate with two faults can be named for the other one. Nothing compares the seed's words for a certificate with two faults: each scenario carries one (R33's seed half, recorded here rather than changed).

kind.description: `root` or `leaf`. **Declared, not enforced**: both ports compare it with `"root"` and judge anything else as a leaf, so a third value is read as `leaf` rather than refused. Narrowing it is a change to the Rust core, which costs a re-pin, so it waits for a change that pays for one.

profile_error.notes: The exact strings of the seed's `x509.mjs profileError`; `null` when the certificate is inside the profile. This is an ANSWER whose one member happens to be called `error`: a failure of the call carries `why` beside it (§0), and this never does.

validate_chain.notes: SPEC §14.2's rules in order. A refusal is an answer, not a failure of the call: `rule` says which one refused. Rule 4 refuses, in this order, `root has expired` (the clock past the root's `notAfter`), `leaf outside its validity`, `leaf longer than 398 days` and `leaf outlives the root`; it never reads the root's `notBefore`.

is_normal_https.notes: An IPv6 literal carries no zone id, in any spelling (`[fe80::1%eth0]`, `[2001:db8::1%25eth0]`): RFC 3986 has none, and the WHATWG parser the seed's `isNormalHttps` uses refuses a `%` inside the brackets. So `address_guard`, chain rule 5, `csr_check`, `ledger_check` and the export's endpoint column refuse one as not the normal form.

address_guard.notes: Refuses a host that is a loopback, link-local, private, unspecified or CGNAT literal (`localhost`, `*.localhost`, `127/8`, `10/8`, `172.16/12`, `192.168/16`, `169.254/16`, `100.64/10`, `0.0.0.0`, `::1`, `::`, `fc00::/7`, `fe80::/10`, deprecated site-local `fec0::/10`, NAT64's local-use `64:ff9b:1::/48`), an IPv6 literal that EMBEDS such an IPv4 address — IPv4-mapped, IPv4-compatible `::/96`, NAT64 `64:ff9b::/96`, 6to4 `2002::/16` — because a translator dials the address inside (`[64:ff9b::7f00:1]` is loopback on a NAT64 network, and a literal has no name to resolve, so this is the whole guard), and, for a guest, an endpoint equal to `self_endpoint`. DNS resolution is the host's; `ip_is_private` is exposed so the host applies the same predicate to what it resolves.

ip_is_private.notes: The predicate `address_guard` applies to a literal host, for the host to apply to what it resolves. One leading `[` and one trailing `]` are dropped, as a URL writes an IPv6 host, and no more. An IPv6 literal with a zone id (`fe80::1%eth0`) is private whatever its address: a zone is an interface scope (RFC 4007 §6), which no global address carries. Text that is no address is not private: an empty zone, and a zone on an IPv4 address, are no address, as Go's `netip` reads them.

dns_name.description: The endpoint's host as a dNSName beside its URI. Absent or null is none; present and empty is refused (`dns_name is empty`).

csr_check.notes: Refuses a bad signature (no proof of possession), a key equal to any root in `root_spkis` (the root-key refusal), an endpoint that is not normal https, an endpoint the address guard refuses. `root_spkis` absent is no roots; present and unreadable is an error, never "no roots to refuse against".

root_cert.description: The root the leaf is issued under, as its certificate (SPEC §2.2): its commonName, key and end date are read from it. It must be a root of the profile and self-signed, and not past its `notAfter` at `now`.

issue_from_csr.notes: Read in this order: `now`; `root_cert`, judged before anything is signed — not a certificate, `parse`; not a root of the profile, `bad_request` `root_cert is not a root of the profile: <why>`; not self-signed, `bad_request` `root_cert is not self-signed`; past its `notAfter` at `now` (RFC 5280's inclusive reading), `root_expired` `the root ended at <instant>: it signs nothing more`; then `root_pkcs8`, which must be the certificate's key (`bad_request` `root_pkcs8 is not the key of root_cert`, after the request is checked); then `root_spkis`, then `csr_check` with the issuing root added to `root_spkis`, then `previous_not_before` and `valid_days`, and the leaf under the monotonic rule. `valid_days` absent is 365; an explicit 0 is refused. A leaf ends no later than its root (SPEC §14.2 rule 4): where the validity asked would run past the root's `notAfter`, `not_after` is the root's and `warnings` says `the leaf ends with its root, at <instant>: sooner than the validity asked`; otherwise `warnings` is empty. A `not_before` the monotonic rule puts after the root's `notAfter` is `root_expired` `the root ends at <instant>, before this leaf could begin`.

root_cert.description: The root the leaf is issued under, as its certificate (SPEC §2.2): its commonName, key and end date are read from it. It must be a root of the profile and self-signed, and not past its `notAfter` at `now`.

issue_tbs_from_csr.notes: As `issue_from_csr`, for the seam, with no `root_pkcs8`: the root's key signs `tbs` elsewhere, and `assemble_leaf` builds the leaf. An expired root is refused before a `tbs` exists, so nothing is ever put in front of a passkey or a card for it.

seal.description: `none`, `optional` or `required` (SPEC §3). **Declared, not enforced**: a non-empty value is written into `X-HDTP-SEAL` as given, so a fourth word makes a card whose policy no reader implements. Narrowing it is a change to the Rust core, which costs a re-pin, so it waits for a change that pays for one. What IS refused is a control character, in this member and every other one a caller supplies.

extra.description: Whole lines, written after the certificate.

card_encode.notes: Folded per RFC 6350 at 75 octets, CRLF, exactly as the seed's `card.mjs`. `extra` present and not a list of strings — a list holding a number or a `null`, or a value that is not a list — is `extra is required`, §0's words for a member of the wrong type. Refuses `<fn|seal|extra> carries a control character`: a card is lines, and a line break in anything a caller supplies writes a property of the caller's choosing (SPEC §3).

ignored.description: Property names the card carried and this library does not read.

card_decode.notes: Every refusal of a card is `bad_request` with the exact `why` strings of `card.mjs`. A `now` that is not an instant is `parse`, `not an RFC 3339 instant: <now>`, as every function that reads an instant answers it (`""` included). An empty `X-HDTP-VERSION` names no version (`no X-HDTP-VERSION`). A card is read by SPEC §3's *Reading a card*, as `card.mjs` reads it: RFC 6350 unfolding (a CRLF or LF followed by one space or tab removed), then `X-HDTP-CERT` takes every following line that does not start a property (`[group.]NAME[;params]:`, the group and name of ASCII letters, digits and `-`), blank lines included, and loses every space, tab, CR and LF; any other line that starts no property is ignored. So a card whose folding a paste damaged reads. What is left is read as every string a port did not write is read (§0), so a stray character, any other whitespace (a vertical tab, a no-break space) or a spare bit set is `certificate does not parse: not base64url`.

pin.description: The half of the host's pin a refresh is judged against.

answer.description: The peer's answer to `get_card`, `{card, card_sig, chain}`, as it was sent: whatever is wrong with it is a refusal of the refresh, never a fault of the call.

renewed.description: The newer leaf the chain proved, and its key, for the pin to become (§14.3); null when the leaf is the pinned one.

root_cert.description: The pinned root's certificate, proved by the chain: what a pin made over a sealed call never had.

refresh_check.notes: Refreshing ONE contact's card (SPEC §3, §14.3), the trust decision both hosts made separately (CW-08): what a peer's answer to `get_card` proves about a pinned contact. A refresh can move a leaf and never a root or an address: the chain is validated against the pinned root and the pinned endpoint. The pin is the host's: `pin` absent or null, or not an object, is `pin is required`, a member absent or of the wrong type is `pin.<member> is required` (`pin.leaf` of the wrong type is `parse` `not base64url`), a `pin.root` that is not a fingerprint is `pin.root is not a fingerprint`, judged as the root is read, before `pin.endpoint`, and a pinned leaf that does not read is an error in its reader's class — read before the answer. `answer` absent or null is `answer is required`; then `now`; then the pinned leaf is parsed, and one that is a CA certificate is `bad_request` `pin.leaf is a CA certificate, not a leaf`: the host's pin, never the peer's answer. The answer is then judged in this order, each refusal `{"ok": false, "why"}`: a `card` and a `card_sig` that are non-empty strings (`the answer to get_card carries no signed card`, an answer that is not an object included); a `chain` of exactly two non-empty strings (`the answer carries <n> certificate(s); get_card answers with the chain, leaf then root (§6.1)`, `n` the length of the list, 0 when it is not one); each member base64url (`a chain member is not base64url`); the card decodes at `now` (`the card does not decode: <card_decode's why>`); it names the pinned root (`the card names another root, not the pinned one`); the chain validates at `now` to the pinned root and endpoint (`the chain it answered with fails rule <n>: <reason>`); its leaf is not older than the pinned one (`the leaf it answered with is superseded by the pinned one (§14.3)`) nor another of the same notBefore (`two different leaves claim the same notBefore (§14.3)`); the card carries that leaf (`the card's certificate is not the leaf the chain proved`); `card_sig` is base64url (`the card signature is not base64url`) and verifies over the card's text under the leaf's key, by `verify`'s rules (`the card signature does not verify under the proven leaf key`).

hpke_seal.notes: `ephemeral_seed` exists for vectors and the intrusion suite; production callers omit it and the core draws 32 fresh bytes. `aad` absent is empty.

recipient_spki.description: The recipient's own public key, as its leaf certificate holds it. It goes into the KEM context (RFC 9180 §4.1) and is never derived from `recipient_pkcs8`; one that is not that key's public key gives another context, and the open fails (`does not open`): it can refuse, never admit.

seal_request.notes: `form` absent is `chain`, which needs `sender_chain`; `method` absent is `tools/call`; `params` absent is `{}`; `exp` absent is `ts + 600`; `cty` absent is a call. `params` is sealed as the value it is, not as the text it was written in: strings as RFC 8785 writes them, an integer the core holds as one (an i64, or a u64 past it) by its digits and every other number as RFC 8785 writes it, members in the order they were written, and a member written twice once, where it first appeared, with the value it was given last (as serde_json's ordered map and `JSON.parse` read it; the core's `canonical::in_order`, Go's `inOrder`). Not sorted: Appendix B's plaintexts write `name` before `arguments`. `ts` and `exp` are integers a header carries as themselves, from −(2^53 − 1) to 2^53 − 1: RFC 8785 writes a number as the double it is, so one past that would be sealed as another. `ts` is judged first, then `exp`, the default included, each `bad_request` `<ts|exp> is an integer from -(2^53 - 1) to 2^53 - 1`; both after the members are read (a 31-byte `ephemeral_seed` is named before them) and before the proof member (a chain of one, or none in the chain form, is named after them).

seal_result.notes: Exactly one of `result` and `error`, sealed as `seal_request` seals `params`. `cty` is `application/hdtp-result+json`. `ts` and `exp` (absent: `ts + 600`) are held as `seal_request` holds them, first.

my_spki.description: The caller's own public key, as its leaf certificate holds it: the header's `kid` is checked against it (`kid is not this key`), and the open puts it in the KEM context. Never derived from `my_pkcs8`; one that names the kid but is not that key's public key does not open.

open_result.notes: The caller side of §13.2: opens, requires `result` xor `error` plus one of `chain`/`leaf`, validates the chain to `expected_root` and `expected_endpoint` or finds the named leaf among `pins`, refuses a superseded leaf, verifies `sig`, checks `cty` and `msg_id`. Every refusal of the ENVELOPE is `{"error": "envelope_invalid", "why"}`. `leaf_update` is a leaf newer than the pin, for the host to store. An absent or null `envelope` is the caller's omission, `bad_request` `envelope is required` (CONTRACT §0); a present one is read for its four members in order (`protected`, `enc`, `ct`, `sig`), and one that is not an object, or lacks a member or holds one that is not a string, is `envelope_invalid` naming it (`envelope is required`, `envelope.sig is required`). `pins` absent or null is none; a pin is read for `root`, `endpoint`, `leaf`, `state` and `leaf_fingerprint` in that order, and one that is not an object or lacks a required member, or holds one of the wrong type, is `bad_request` naming it by its path (`pins[0] is required`, `pins[0].root is required`), and a `root` that is not a fingerprint is `pins[<i>].root is not a fingerprint`, a `state` other than the three `pins[<i>].state is active, pending_out or blocked`, and a `leaf_fingerprint` that is not a fingerprint `pins[<i>].leaf_fingerprint is not a fingerprint`, as a node's pin is. A chain in the plaintext with a member that is not a string, or does not read as base64url, is `envelope_invalid` `plaintext shape`, as in `decide`. The first pin for the chain's root is the one read, as `decide` reads a node's pins; a pin whose leaf does not read is an error of the call in its reader's class (`parse`; `unsupported` for a key outside the profile), never `superseded leaf`.

follow_renewed.notes: §14.4: `answer` is the peer's `{"code": "certificate_renewed", "data": {"chain"}}`, whatever it actually sent. Validate to the pinned root and the dialed address, and follow only when the chain is newer than or equal to the pin.

chain.description: The chain the caller proved outside an envelope — at the TLS layer, where the handshake is its leaf key's signature: leaf, then root.

decide_chain.notes: §5.1's pin decision on its own, for a host's TLS door: the part of `decide` after the chain is validated and signed for, written once in each port and taken by both functions, so a chain presented at the TLS layer earns exactly what an envelope carrying it would (N1, N2: the node's TLS door read the removal tombstone in the states `decide` does not, and served a conflicting leaf as a guest). Read as `decide` reads its arguments: `node`, `chain` and `now` absent or null, in that order; the node whole, as `decide` reads it; the chain, as every function reads one (not a list: `chain is required`; a member that is not a base64url string: `parse` `not base64url`); `now`. The chain is validated at `now` with no expectation; one that fails is `envelope_invalid` `chain rule <n>: <reason>`. Then the pins, in `decide`'s order: no pin for the root — a tombstone for it (the first) within 30 days whose leaf the chain's is newer than is `pending_new_address` forced `ask` with a `pending` effect (`returned after removal`), and otherwise a guest (`unknown root`); a blocked pin is a guest (`blocked`); a leaf older than the pinned one a guest (`superseded leaf`); a different leaf of the pinned one's notBefore `envelope_invalid` (`a different leaf with the same notBefore`); another endpoint is `pending_new_address` under `ask` and, under `auto`, a re-pin with the former endpoint recorded and a `new_address` event; a newer leaf at the pinned endpoint a `pin_update` and a `renewal` event; then `pending` for a `pending_out` pin and `contact` otherwise. A guest carries `why`, `demote` and `address_claim`, as `decide`'s does. What is the call's — a guest's tools and card, the receiver's own address (§14.5), what a `pending_out` pin may call — the host applies to each call, as `decide` applies it to the envelope's. There is no `seen`. Node state that does not read is an error of the call in its reader's class, as in `decide`.

vault_seal.notes: `plaintext` is a VaultPlaintext or a RecordPlaintext, and its `v` is 1: anything else is `bad_request` (`a vault plaintext is v 1: the root, or the record`). The plaintext is sealed as `seal_request` seals `params`, as the value it is. That generation is all `vault_seal` checks of the plaintext (and `vault_open` of what it opens): the two shapes are held by `wallet_issue`, where the rules read them, so a stricter seal or open cannot lock a person out of a document a wallet already keeps. Read in this order: `passphrase` (absent: `passphrase is required`; empty: `empty passphrase`), `plaintext` and its generation, then `kdf`, `salt` and `nonce`, then the nonce's length (`vault`, `nonce is 12 bytes`) and the salt's (`vault`, `salt is at least 8 bytes`: `VaultSaltMin`). `kdf` absent or null is `KdfDefault`, and one that is not an object is `bad_request` `kdf is required`. An object is read by the one reader `vault_open` reads a document's `kdf` with, except that a member left out takes the default: a `name` other than `argon2id`, or one that is not a string, is `vault` `unknown kdf`; a parameter that is not a whole number written as one (`1.0`, `-0`, `"8192"`), or is outside its range, is `vault` `kdf parameters out of range`, never truncated; and a member other than those four, named in any case but theirs, is `vault` `kdf holds name, m_kib, t and p, and nothing else: <member>`. `salt` and `nonce` are for tests only.

vault_open.notes: Read in this order: `vault` (absent or null: `vault is required`), `passphrase` (absent: `passphrase is required`), then the document's header, where it does not read, all `vault`: a document that is not an object, or whose `format` is not `hdtp-vault/1`, is `not an hdtp-vault/1 document`; its `kdf` is read by the one reader `vault_seal`'s is, with all four members (`Kdf`): one that is not an object, or whose `name` is absent, not a string or not `argon2id`, is `unknown kdf`, a parameter that is absent, not a whole number written as one, or outside its range is `kdf parameters out of range`, and another member is `kdf holds name, m_kib, t and p, and nothing else: <member>`; `salt`, `nonce` and `ct` that are absent or not strings are no bytes, and one that is not base64url, or a nonce that is not 12 bytes, is the one message below; then a salt under `VaultSaltMin` bytes is `salt is at least 8 bytes`. A wrong passphrase and a tampered document are one message (`the passphrase is wrong or the vault is damaged`). A document that opens to a plaintext whose `v` is not 1 is of another generation and is refused (`vault`, `this vault is of another generation and is not opened: there is no conversion`); nothing converts.

wallet_issue.notes: Two documents, as §9 keeps them: the vault is the root and nothing else, the record holds the ledger this reads and the entry answered is appended to. A vault carrying `ledger` or `contacts` is refused (`bad_request`, `a vault holds the root and nothing else: its ledger and contacts belong in the record`); an absent or null document is `vault_plaintext is required` or `record_plaintext is required` (CONTRACT §0), and a record that is not an object `record_plaintext is required: the ledger lives there`. After `root_fingerprint`, `csr`, `now` and `valid_days` (present and not an integer: `valid_days is required`), each document is held to its schema before anything in it is read, as follows. Inside both documents, as in the arguments (CONTRACT §0), a member the document declares that is `null` is absent — an optional one is not there, a required one is named as a missing one is — and a member it does not declare is refused whatever it holds, `null` included (a vault's `ledger: null` is a vault carrying a ledger). The vault: not an object, `vault_plaintext is required: the root lives there`; then its `v`; then the first member, in sorted order, it does not hold, `vault_plaintext holds v, roots, prf and passkey, and nothing else: <member>`; then its `roots` (absent or not a list: `the vault's roots is a list`), each entry a `VaultRoot` (`the vault's root <i> does not read: <member>`: the first of `fingerprint`, `cn`, `cert` and `created` that is absent, not a string, not a fingerprint or not an instant, then an `alg`, `pkcs8`, `holder` or `rebound_at` of the wrong type, then the first member, in sorted order, it does not hold; an entry that is not an object, `the vault's root <i> does not read`); then its `prf` (32 bytes, or `the vault's prf does not read`) and its `passkey` (an object holding `credential_id`, a string, and nothing else, or `the vault's passkey does not read`). Then the record, likewise: `record_plaintext holds v, roots, ledger, contacts, passkey and backup_verified_at, and nothing else: <member>`; its `roots` where present, as the vault's (`the record's roots is a list`, `the record's root <i> does not read: <member>`); its `ledger` (not a list: `the record's ledger is a list`) and every ledger entry, every root's: an entry that is not an object, lacks a required member, has one of the wrong type, a `root` that is not a fingerprint, an empty `endpoint` or an instant that does not parse, or carries one it does not hold is refused (`the record's ledger entry <i> does not read: <member>`), never skipped — skipped, it could be the live leaf; its `contacts` (not a list: `the record's contacts is a list`), each entry a `VaultContact` (`the record's contact <i> does not read: <member>`: `root` absent or not a fingerprint, `endpoint` absent or not a string, a `name`, `leaf`, `root_cert` or `added` that is not a string or, for `added`, not an instant, then the first member, in sorted order, it does not hold; an entry that is not an object, `the record's contact <i> does not read`); its `passkey` (`the record's passkey does not read`) and its `backup_verified_at`, a whole number (`the record's backup_verified_at does not read`). A root with no `pkcs8` is refused (`this root is held on a card: wallet_issue signs only with a key the vault holds`), and one whose `pkcs8` does not read is refused in its reader's class (`parse`; `unsupported` for a key outside the profile). Then SPEC §2.2, before anything is signed: a root whose entry's `cert` reads and is past its `notAfter` at `now` is refused as `issue_from_csr` refuses it (`root_expired`), before the proof of possession below; the key's fingerprint is `root_fingerprint` (`the vault's root key is not the root it is filed under`); the entry's `cert` reads (in its reader's class) and holds the key (`the vault's root certificate is not its key's`); and the key signs `HDTP root proof v1`, a newline and 32 random bytes, verified under the certificate's key (`the vault's root key does not sign for its certificate`). After issuing, the chain of the leaf and that certificate is validated at `now` against `root_fingerprint` and the request's endpoint before it is answered (`the chain it issued does not validate: chain rule <n>: <reason>`). The entry answered is the endpoint and the dates, never the leaf. The wallet's rules: `csr_check` with the vault's roots as `root_spkis`; then `ledger_check`'s rules over the record's ledger (a record with no `ledger` has no entry to read): `new_host` true when no ledger entry names that endpoint's host, with the warning `new host: this endpoint's host has never been issued to`; the **live leaf is the newest one issued** (§14.3) and a second endpoint while it is unexpired is refused unless `move: true`, which instead warns `move: the live leaf at the previous endpoint is superseded once contacts see this one` (a `move` or a `move_back`); `not_before` monotonic over the ledger; `valid_days` absent means 365 and an explicit 0 is refused. A leaf ends no later than its root, and `warnings` then carries `issue_from_csr`'s line saying so.

ledger.description: The record's ledger, every root's entries. Absent or null: the signer has no record, so no ledger to read (`no_ledger`); `[]` is a ledger with nothing in it.

endpoint.description: The request's endpoint, in the normal form of SPEC §14.1: `csr_check`'s `endpoint`.

move.description: The person chose to move (or to move back). Absent is false. It changes `refusal` and nothing else.

refusal.description: SPEC §9's one live leaf per identity: `a leaf is live for <endpoint>: a second endpoint is a move, not a second home`, when a leaf is live at another endpoint and `move` is not true. Null otherwise.

new_host.description: No entry of this root names the endpoint's host. True with no ledger.

known_endpoint.description: An entry of this root names exactly this endpoint. False with no ledger.

previous_not_before.description: The latest `not_before` issued to this root: the next leaf's must be later.

until.description: `move` and `move_back`: the live leaf's `not_after`, until which contacts not yet reached keep using `from`.

ledger_check.notes: The wallet's ledger rules, as facts, in the one place they are written: `wallet_issue` applies them, the `hdtp` CLI applies them for a card-held root, and a wallet page or a host renders the move notice from them. In order: `root` (absent or empty: `root is required`), `endpoint`, `now`, `move` (present and not a boolean: `move is required`); then `endpoint` not in normal form is refused (`endpoint is not an https URL in normal form`); then every ledger entry, every root's, is read as `wallet_issue` reads it (`the record's ledger is a list`; `the record's ledger entry <i> does not read: <member>`, a `root` that is not a fingerprint and an empty `endpoint` included) — an entry that does not read is REFUSED, a `not_before` that does not parse included, never skipped: skipped, it could be the live leaf. The **live leaf** is this root's newest entry by `not_before` (§14.3; the first of equals, in ledger order), if its `not_after` is after `now`; an older entry still in its validity is history, not live. `notice.kind`: with no ledger, `no_ledger`; a leaf live at another endpoint, `move_back` when this endpoint has been issued to before and `move` when it has not (both with `from` and `until`, the live leaf's endpoint and `not_after`); otherwise `renew` when this endpoint has been issued to, and `new_host` when it has not. The kind does not depend on `move`; only `refusal` does.

request.description: A SigningRequest as it arrived: held to that schema by this function, which names what is wrong, rather than by the caller.

origin.description: The request's `Origin` header, as the browser serialised it.

root_spkis.description: The roots the wallet holds, for `csr_check`'s root-key refusal. Absent is none; present and unreadable is an error.

csr.description: The request's `csr` member, exactly as given: not re-encoded.

signing_request_check.notes: What a web wallet decides about a host's signing request before a person sees it. The arguments first: `request` absent or not an object, `origin` absent or not a string, `now` absent (each `<name> is required`), `now` unreadable (`parse`), `root_spkis` unreadable — these are errors. Everything about the request itself is `{ok: false, why}`, the first thing wrong, in this order: a member a request does not carry (the first in sorted order: `a signing request does not carry <m>`); a member that is not a string (`<m> is a string, as a form carries it`) or over its bound (`<m> is longer than <n>`), in the order of SigningRequest's members; a required member absent or empty (`<m> is required`); an `origin` empty or `null` (`the request has no origin: a wallet answers only the origin that asked`); the redirect — not ASCII without spaces or backslashes (`the redirect is not an absolute URL`), a fragment (`the redirect carries a fragment`), not `https://` or `http://` (`the redirect is not https, or http to a loopback host`), userinfo (`the redirect carries userinfo`), a host not in lower-case normal form — IPv6 hex in lower case, a name of labels none of which is empty (`the redirect's host is not in normal form`), a port that is not 1–65535 without a leading zero (`the redirect's port is not in normal form`), `http` to a host that is not `localhost`, a dotted quad in `127.0.0.0/8` in normal form, or `[::1]` (`the redirect is not https, or http to a loopback host`); the redirect's origin (`scheme://host[:port]`, the default port left out) not equal to `origin` (`the redirect's origin is not the origin that asked`); `expires` not an RFC 3339 UTC instant in the one grammar — upper-case `T` and `Z`, `.` alone before a fraction (`expires is not an RFC 3339 instant`), not after `now` (`the request has expired`), or more than 600 seconds after it (`the request expires more than ten minutes ahead`); `purpose` not `renew` or `move` (`purpose is renew or move`; `signup` is not taken from a host); `valid_days` not a whole number 1–398 without a leading zero (`valid_days is a whole number of days from 1 to 398`); `state` not 43 base64url characters of 32 bytes (`state is 32 bytes, base64url`); `expect_root` not `sha256:` and 43 base64url characters (`expect_root is not a root fingerprint`); `root_cert`, when present, not base64url, not a certificate, not a root of §14.1's profile, or not the root `expect_root` names; `csr` not base64url (`csr is not base64url`); then `csr_check` with `root_spkis`, whose refusal is answered in its words. What stays the wallet's: proving the root against `expect_root` (§2.2), showing the asking origin, the `recipient` as the host's claim, the endpoint, the validity and whether the host is new, and the validity the person chooses. Nothing of the request is kept.

manifest.description: manifest.json's text, exactly as its bytes decode.

threads_csv.description: Required when the file has threads.csv; refused when it has none.

export_read.notes: SPEC §9.2's validation of everything but the messages and the media bytes, refusing the whole file at the first fault; every refusal of the file is `bad_request` whose `why` names the member, then the row (the header is row 1) and the column. In order: each directory entry, in the order given (a name that is not exactly `manifest.json`, `contacts.csv`, `threads.csv`, `messages.jsonl`, `media/` or `media/` and 64 lowercase hex: `entry "<name>": not a name an export holds`; `appears twice`; `encrypted`; a symbolic link; a directory but `media/`; a stated size over its bound); `manifest.json` and `contacts.csv` present; the manifest (exactly its members, `hdtp_export` 1, `owner` a fingerprint and the importing identity's, the counts whole numbers, `owner_name` and `tool` holding no private key, `files` naming only the text members — `contacts.csv`, `threads.csv`, `messages.jsonl` — each a lowercase hex sha256, never a media member, which is bound by its name and counted); every text member but the manifest listed in `files`, and every listed member present; `threads.csv`, `messages.jsonl` and `media/` present when counted; the media entries as many as counted; `contacts.csv` (its sha256, its header exactly, at most 5000 rows, each row's cells — a cell that holds a private key is refused before its column's rule — the root a fingerprint, unique, not the owner; the endpoint in normal form and passing the address guard; names at most 200 characters; the status; `true` or `false`; §8's permissions, single-spaced, none twice; the leaf a leaf and the root certificate a root of §14.1's profile, the latter for the row's root; `added` an instant) and its count; then `threads.csv` the same way, under one of two headers: `id,contact,topic,created_at,last_at`, where every contact is a root in `contacts.csv` (`names no contact in contacts.csv`), or that and `contact_name,contact_display_name`, when the file holds a removed thread: a thread whose contact is no root of `contacts.csv`, a fingerprint and not the owner, its names at most 200 characters and the same on every removed thread of that root (`not what an earlier removed thread of this contact says`), while any other thread's names are empty; the longer header with no removed thread is refused (`threads.csv: row 1: the header names contact_name and contact_display_name, and no thread is a removed thread`). A header that is neither is refused naming both (`threads.csv: row 1: the header is not id,contact,topic,created_at,last_at, nor that and contact_name,contact_display_name`). Ids are unique. A removed thread is answered with its two names, any other thread without them. Before either CSV member is parsed, a member holding more than 65536 characters below U+0020 but tab, line feed and carriage return is refused (`<member>: <n> characters below U+0020 but tab, line feed and carriage return, over the 65536 this library takes in one member`): this library's ceiling, as a host's own (SPEC §9.2), since this answer writes each as six bytes (`\u00XX`), or two for U+0008 and U+000C. One leading `'` is stripped from every cell. A row's `leaf` is answered only when `[leaf, root_cert]` validates at the row's endpoint at `now` (§14.2); otherwise it is null and pins nothing. `media` is each media member's hash and stated size, sorted by hash: the host checks each file's bytes against both as it streams it.

contacts.description: The roots a message may name: export_read's contacts', and its removed threads' contacts.

first_line.description: The line number of `lines[0]` in the whole member. Absent is 1.

media_seen.description: The media these messages name, sorted, once each.

export_read_messages.notes: One batch of messages.jsonl's lines as the host streams it (each line without its `\n`). Each line: at most 65536 bytes, one JSON object, exactly the members of a message (a stranger first, then a missing one), no member holding a private key, then each member's rule: `id` and `msg_id` not empty, `thread` and `contact` naming the file's, `direction`, `sender`, `time`, `body` at most 16384 bytes, `reply_to` a msg_id or null, `status`, and `attachments` at most one, each exactly `{file, filename, mime, size}` naming a media member; a message with an attachment has an empty body. A refusal is `messages.jsonl: line <n>, member <m>: <why>`. What only the whole member can decide is export_read_end's.

messages_sha256.description: The sha256 of messages.jsonl's bytes as the host streamed them; null when the file has no messages.jsonl.

media.description: The file's media members, by hash: export_read's `media`. Each must be named by a message.

export_read_end.notes: SPEC §9.2's rules across the whole of messages.jsonl, once it is streamed: the line count against `counts.messages`, the member's sha256 against `files`, `id` unique in the file, every `reply_to` naming a `msg_id` in the file, and every media member (`media`, the hashes export_read answered) named by some attachment (`media/<h>: nothing names it`). `lines` absent or null is `lines is required`, and one that is not a whole number `lines is a whole number`.

partial.description: The manifest without the messages: counts.messages 0 and no messages.jsonl in files, for export_manifest to finish.

threads_csv.description: Null when there are no threads: the member is then left out, as §9.2 allows when it counts zero.

export_write.notes: The canonical members, the same bytes from every port: each row checked by the reader's rules (`contacts[<i>], column <c>: <why>`), contacts sorted by root and threads by id, a permission list sorted, instants written as RFC 3339 UTC seconds, every cell that begins with `=` `+` `-` `@` `'` a tab or a carriage return written with one `'` before it, a cell quoted exactly when it holds `,` `"` CR or LF, CRLF after every record. What a contact controls never stops the export (SPEC §9.2): every name (`name`, `display_name`, `contact_name`, `contact_display_name`) and a thread's `topic` lose every character below U+0020 but tab, line feed and carriage return, before a name's length is checked; an `id` is written as given, so a host that takes a thread id holding them may write a file the reader's ceiling refuses; `their_permissions` keeps only the names of §8, once each, and `display_name`, a contact's or a removed thread's `contact_display_name`, is cut to 200 characters, on a character; the reader refuses both as written by anyone else. A thread whose contact is no contact is a removed thread and carries its former contact's names, the same on every thread of that root (`threads[<i>], column contact_name: not what an earlier removed thread of this contact says`); non-empty names on any other thread are refused. `threads_csv` has the longer header, with `contact_name,contact_display_name`, only when a removed thread is among the threads: every other file is the file a writer without removed threads writes. `owner_name` or `tool` holding a private key is refused, naming the member (`owner_name holds a private key`). The manifest's `files` lists the text members only; the media are counted. A book is this with no threads and no media.

msg_ids.description: The msg_id of every message the file carries, when the host writes it in batches. Absent: the messages of this call, less those left out.

left_out.description: Every message left out, by its id and the reason, for the host to report to the person (SPEC §9.2).

export_write_messages.notes: One line per message, in the order given, as RFC 8785 JSON; each message held to the reader's rules but its references, which the host holds (`messages[<i>], member <m>: <why>`). What a contact controls never stops the export (SPEC §9.2): a message whose `body` holds what reads as a private key is left out, not refused, and listed in `left_out` (`its body holds what reads as a private key, which an export never carries`) — the host leaves out the file it carried too; and a `reply_to` naming a message the file does not carry (not among `msg_ids`, or, without them, not among the messages written) is written `null`. Key material in any other member is refused. The host writes each line followed by `\n`, hashes the member's bytes and counts its lines for export_manifest.

messages.description: The lines written to messages.jsonl. Absent is 0.

export_manifest.notes: export_write's partial manifest finished with what the host counted and hashed: held to the manifest's rules first, refused if it already counts or lists messages, `messages.jsonl` required in `hashes` when there are messages.

held.description: The contacts the importing host holds, as rows.

export_merge.notes: SPEC §9.2's import step 2: an imported leaf never replaces a pin the host validated itself (§14.5). A row whose root is not held is written; a row whose root is held WITHOUT a leaf is written when the row carries one (export_read kept it only because it validated); and what the person decided about that contact stays as held: a blocked contact stays blocked, and its `permissions` stay the ones granted. Every other held root is kept as held. Each of the endpoint, leaf and root certificate a row would change, and each of the `status` and `permissions` (a list compared as a set), is a conflict for the host to show. A held row or a row is refused, `bad_request` naming it, for a `root` that is not a fingerprint (`held[<i>]: root is not a fingerprint`), a `status` other than the three (`rows[<i>]: status is not active, blocked or pending_out`: a held `Blocked` was read as not blocked, so the import did not keep the block) and an `added` that is not an instant (`held[<i>]: added is not an RFC 3339 instant`), export_read's words; the rows' other members are read for what the merge needs.

contacts.description: The wallet's book, as the record keeps it.

book_rows.notes: The wallet's book as rows of contacts.csv, the one mapping every wallet uses (SPEC §9.2: a book is an export of contacts only). Each contact, in order: an object (`contacts[<i>] is an object`), no member but `root`, `endpoint`, `name`, `leaf`, `root_cert` and `added` (the first other, in sorted order: `contacts[<i>]: "<m>" is not a member of a wallet contact`), `root` and `endpoint` strings (`contacts[<i>]: <m> is required`), the rest strings when present (`contacts[<i>]: <m> is a string`), then a `root` that is a fingerprint (`contacts[<i>]: root is not a fingerprint`) and an `added`, when present, that is an instant (`contacts[<i>]: added is not an RFC 3339 instant`): both reach the row as its root and its `added`, which the contract types. A row carries the root, the endpoint, the name (empty when absent), the leaf and the root certificate (null when absent), and `added` (the export's time when absent); its other columns are what a contact the wallet keeps is: an empty `display_name`, `status` `active`, `was_active` true, and nothing granted either way. The rows are not otherwise checked here: export_write holds each to the reader's rules.

bytes.description: A media file's bytes, all of them.

holds_private_key.description: The bytes are a private key in DER, PKCS #8 or SEC1 by shape whatever the algorithm, or are UTF-8 text holding one: PEM armour naming a private key, or a word (split at ASCII whitespace) that decodes as base64 or base64url to one.

media_holds_private_key.notes: SPEC §9.2's key material over a media file, the check CONTRACT §6.2 leaves to a host because the core never sees a file: every port's export reader judges a media file by it, and a host that streams media asks it here rather than keeping a copy. It reads leniently, as a lenient decoder would: a word forgives its padding, either alphabet and a last character whose spare bits are set, and a DER length may take any definite form of up to four octets, minimal or not, so that nothing a person's tools read as a key is passed as none. `js/key-material.json` is the list of cases.

rules.description: A rules document, as a host's configuration holds it; anything at all, since this is what checks it.

limits_rules_check.notes: Whether a rules document can be enforced as written, and the first reason it cannot, in this order: not an object (`the limits rules are an object`); a member it does not hold, the first in sorted order (`the limits rules hold <members>, and nothing else: <member>`); each member in the order of `LimitsRules`, absent or not a number (`<member> is a number`); then every number finite, `contact_calls_per_second` above 0 (`… is above 0`) and every other at least 1 (`… is at least 1`); `pending_in_cap` whole (`pending_in_cap is a whole number`); and a contact's bucket refilling from empty within the hour (`contact_burst / contact_calls_per_second is at most 3600: …`). `rules` absent or null is `bad_request`, `rules is required`. A host publishes no document this refuses.

state.description: The rows the host holds, by bucket key: at least the charge's. Absent or null is none, and a bucket with no row is full.

retry_after.description: 0 when allowed; when refused by a bucket, the whole seconds, at least 1, until every refusing bucket holds a call again (to within a second's rounding, as the cloud's arithmetic has it); null when refused by `pending_in_cap`, which no wait refills.

refused_by.description: The key of the bucket that needs longest, the first of equals in charge order, or `pending_in`; null when allowed.

writes.description: The rows to store, in charge order: every bucket of an allowed call, none of a refusal.

limits_decide.notes: SPEC §12's call budgets as one decision (crates/hdtp-limits; go/limits.go). A call is charged one token in EVERY bucket of its charge, or in none: a refusal spends nothing. A bucket's level is `min(burst, tokens + elapsed × rate)`, `elapsed` the seconds since `updated_at` and never negative (a clock that went back refills nothing, and the row is written with the earlier time); a level under 1 refuses, with `retry_after = max(1, ceil((1 − level) / rate))`. The arithmetic is what the cloud's `RateLimiter.take` was, operation for operation in IEEE double precision, until the cloud removed it and decided through this function (batondeck ba68f9c); `js/cases/limits-vectors.json`, a fixed record of that TypeScript's decisions, holds every port to the same decisions and the same bits. A host may delete a row idle for over an hour: under rules `limits_rules_check` passes it is full, and no decision changes. In order: `rules` (absent: `rules is required`; not enforceable: `the limits rules cannot be enforced: <limits_rules_check's why>`), `charge` (not an object: `charge is required`; `charge.kind is required`; `charge.kind is one of …`; a member its kind does not hold, the first in sorted order: `a <kind> charge holds <members>, and nothing else: <member>`; `charge.<member> is required` for a string that is absent or empty, `charge.<member> is a whole number` for a count, `charge.root is a string or null`, `charge.source is required`, `charge.addressed is required`), `now` (absent or null: `now is required`; otherwise `now is a time in milliseconds`: a whole number from 0 to 2^53 − 1, written without a fraction or an exponent), `state` (not an object: `state is an object of rows by bucket`; a row, in sorted order of key, that does not read: `the state's row <key> does not read: <member>`).

key.description: The row's key, as `limits_decide`'s `state` and `writes` name it.

per_second.description: The sustained rate, in calls a second: for `identity` and `out:identity`, `contact_cap` × `contact_calls_per_second`, at most `identity_capacity_per_second` and at least 1.

burst.description: The most calls the bucket holds; a bucket with no row is full.

buckets.description: The buckets the charge is charged to, in charge order; none for `pending_in`, a count.

limits_buckets.notes: The rows `limits_decide` reads for a charge, so a host can fetch them before it asks: the key scheme `LimitsCharge` describes, from the one place it is written (crates/hdtp-limits `Charge::buckets`; go/limits.go `Buckets`), where a host on the Wasm had to derive it a second time. Reads `rules` and then `charge` exactly as `limits_decide` does, in its words (`rules is required`; `the limits rules cannot be enforced: <why>`; the charge's own refusals).
